extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in Donald Trump's use of social media, platform moderation, and related legal/political issues
extracted.subtask_short: Wikipedia article: use of X by Trump
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of Donald Trump's activity on Twitter/X, covering tweet content, follower dynamics, moderation actions, legal and archival treatment of tweets, and notable controversies and incidents. The page summarizes platform policies and governmental/legal responses as applied to Trump's posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twitter rule against threats of violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter has a rule against making threats of violence; tweets that threaten destruction or violent action (e.g., threats toward North Korea) are assessed under this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Twitter cited its rule against threats when evaluating Trump's tweets about totally destroying #NoKo and explained that factors such as newsworthiness and public interest were considered when deciding whether such tweets violated the rule; Twitter acknowledged its internal guidelines and planned updates to public rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twitter 'Hateful Conduct' policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy prohibiting accounts and content that promote hateful conduct; used to suspend or remove accounts that violate the policy (example: Katie Hopkins' account suspension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes enforcement examples — accounts sharing hateful material can be permanently suspended under this policy; Trump's retweets of material later judged hateful prompted criticism and platform actions against originating accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twitter 'Civic Integrity' policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules governing misinformation and content that may undermine civic processes (e.g., false claims about voting, elections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tweets falsely suggesting postal voting would compromise elections were either removed or labeled as disputed; enforcement included labeling, deletion requests, account locking, and permanent suspension for repeated/severe violations tied to civic integrity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness/public interest exception in moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms may weigh newsworthiness or public interest when deciding whether to remove or leave up content that might otherwise violate rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter explicitly cited newsworthiness and public interest as factors in whether a tweet violated policies, sometimes leaving contested tweets visible for their public relevance while acknowledging internal guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood to inspire replication or encourage violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether a user's posts are likely to inspire others to commit violent acts or replicate harmful behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter justified permanent suspension of Trump's account by stating his continued tweeting was 'likely to inspire others to replicate the violent acts that took place on January 6, 2021' and cited 'multiple indicators' showing tweets were understood as encouragement; this standard was pivotal for escalation from labeling to suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural enforcement mechanisms (delete/label/lock/suspend)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific platform actions and thresholds used to enforce rules: labeling disputed tweets, deleting tweets, locking accounts pending deletion, and suspending or permanently banning accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: Twitter required deletion of three specific tweets to unlock Trump's account (with a subsequent 12-hour waiting period); it permanently suspended accounts for repeated/severe violations; platforms may also reinstate accounts later under different ownership or policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of tweets as presidential records / official statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether tweets by a sitting president constitute presidential records or official statements affects archival obligations and legal status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. National Archives said Trump's tweets are presidential records; the Department of Justice argued tweets were 'official statements of the President' in some cases and 'personal conduct' in others. The article notes limited caselaw on how government social media use is treated as a 'public forum' under the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether tweets constitute formal orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination whether a tweet functions as a formal, self-executing order requiring government action (vs. rhetoric or personal statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials and courts have differed: the Secretary of the Navy said he did not interpret a tweet as a formal order; in other cases courts have sought clarification from the White House. The article highlights ambiguity and case-by-case analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegality under international law (targeting cultural sites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements threatening deliberate targeting of cultural sites can implicate international law and be classified as war crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Trump's tweet threatening '52 Iranian sites (important to Iran & the Iranian culture) ... HIT VERY FAST AND VERY HARD' would, if acted upon, have constituted a war crime by deliberately targeting cultural heritage. The page uses this as a legal standard for assessing the gravity of certain threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification/retweeting of extremist or misleading content as endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Retweeting or amplifying posts from extremist, white supremacist, or conspiratorial accounts is treated as promotion or endorsement and can lead to public condemnation and platform action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents multiple instances where Trump retweeted extremist, racist, or conspiratorial material (e.g., Britain First videos, neo‑Nazi-sourced fake statistics), leading to outrage, suspension of the source accounts, and debates about amplification as de facto endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incitement to harassment and real-world harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that insults, targets individuals (including private citizens), or encourages harassment can lead to online abuse and offline consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites research (one in eight posts as personal insults) and examples where tweets directed at individuals precipitated waves of online harassment and threatening communications; such harms inform judgments about appropriateness and moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misinformation about elections and civic processes
rubrics_metrics.description: False claims about election integrity, vote counting, or officials' powers are subject to moderation and can be labeled/removed under platform policies addressing civic misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include tweets falsely claiming the Vice President could reject electors or urging delays to elections; platforms labeled, removed, or otherwise acted on such tweets during 2020–2021 under civic integrity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account authenticity and follower legitimacy (bots/fake followers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of follower quality (real vs. fake/bot accounts) affects assessments of reach and influence; high proportions of bots may distort perceived support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites analyses indicating significant proportions of Trump's followers were fake or bots, and notes platform crackdowns on fake accounts reduced follower counts; this criterion is used in evaluating social-media influence metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform internal guidance vs. public-facing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms maintain internal guidelines that may differ from or supplement public policy documents; enforcement can rely on these internal criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter acknowledged that factors like newsworthiness and other internal considerations influenced enforcement decisions and committed to updating public-facing rules to reflect such practices; this distinction matters when evaluating why certain content is left up or removed.
